query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase high-entropy alloy, even minute intentional additions of impurity elements (e.g., P or S) will segregate to microstructural defect sites during intermediate-temperature aging, locally weakening atomic bonds and thus lowering the material’s toughness, leading to brittle behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Modified CoCrFeMnNi high‐entropy alloy with a uniform, primarily single‐phase microstructure and very low baseline levels of impurities.
generation.intervention: Introduce 0.1–0.5 wt% of controlled impurity elements during alloy synthesis followed by aging at 400–600°C under a controlled atmosphere.
generation.conditions: Conduct a side‐by‐side comparison between the impurity-doped HEA and a nominally pure HEA baseline, ensuring identical processing and aging conditions to isolate the effect of impurity segregation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nano-scale impurity segregation occurring at microstructural defects such as dislocation cores and coherent interfaces.
generation.mechanism: During intermediate-temperature aging, the introduced impurities diffuse and preferentially segregate to existing microstructural defects. This local enrichment alters the bonding environment and disrupts the cooperative plastic deformation mechanism, leading to premature crack nucleation and a shift from ductile to brittle fracture behavior, despite the alloy remaining single-phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Doped and aged HEA specimens will display observable nano-scale impurity decoration at defect sites (as evidenced by high-resolution TEM/EDS) and a measurable reduction in toughness (e.g., lower fracture stress and more brittle fracture modes) compared to the pure HEA baseline. If the impurities fail to segregate or do not affect mechanical properties, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
generation.baseline: Pure CoCrFeMnNi HEA synthesized under identical conditions without intentional impurity additions and subjected to the same aging protocol, expected to retain higher toughness and a uniform microstructure.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to be most pronounced at intermediate service temperatures (400–600°C) where diffusion is sufficient for impurity migration. At significantly lower or higher temperatures, either the kinetic drive for segregation may be too weak or other degradation processes could dominate, respectively.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the precise extent and distribution of impurity segregation and its quantitative effect on toughness degradation, as these factors may be sensitive to the exact impurity type, concentration, and aging duration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA specimens: one set with controlled 0.1–0.5 wt% impurity doping and one pure set. Subject both to aging at 400–600°C for predetermined durations. Characterize the microstructure using high-resolution TEM/EDS to assess impurity segregation, and perform standardized fracture toughness tests on both sample sets.
measurements: Nano-scale analysis of impurity distribution via TEM/EDS
Fracture toughness (e.g., critical stress intensity factor measurements)
Comparison of crack initiation and propagation behavior
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the impurity-doped specimens do not exhibit significantly enhanced impurity segregation at defect sites or fail to show a statistically significant reduction in toughness relative to the pure HEA baseline, then the hypothesis that trace impurities trigger brittle behavior in HEAs will be falsified.

proposals.intervention: Systematic thermal aging experiments to accelerate grain-boundary diffusion
proposals.conditions: Expose single-phase HEA specimens to isothermal holds at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 600–800°C) for varying times under inert atmosphere
proposals.structural_mediator: Local grain-boundary elemental segregation and incipient short-range order
proposals.mechanism: Even in a single-phase HEA, prolonged exposure can drive subtle segregation at grain boundaries where slower diffusion kinetics cause local chemical fluctuations. This segregation reduces grain-boundary cohesion, promoting intergranular crack nucleation under load, a departure from conventional alloy precipitation phenomena.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated baselines, aged specimens will show measurable increases in localized elemental enrichment (via APT or TEM-EDS) at grain boundaries together with a drop in toughness (transition from ductile to brittle intergranular fracture) in standardized fracture tests. In contrast, similar tests in conventional alloys would show pronounced intermetallic precipitates rather than subtle segregation.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction tests whether toughness degradation in HEAs arises from grain-boundary chemical redistribution—not overt precipitate formation—and it provides a controlled thermal exposure comparison that distinguishes the behavior from conventional alloys.

proposals.intervention: Mechanical cycling at cryogenic temperatures combined with in-situ diffraction measurements
proposals.conditions: Subject specimens to cyclic loading at cryogenic conditions (e.g., liquid nitrogen temperature) while monitoring microstructural evolution using neutron or synchrotron X-ray diffraction
proposals.structural_mediator: Strain-induced short-range ordering (SRO) within the lattice
proposals.mechanism: Under high strain at low temperatures, dislocation interactions may trigger local reordering of atoms in the otherwise random solid solution. Such SRO lowers dislocation mobility and may form brittle clusters that act as crack nucleation sites, differing from the conventional precipitation seen in traditional alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to room-temperature deformation, cryogenic cycling will promote detectable SRO (observed as subtle diffraction changes) that correlates with a reduction in ductility and a shift toward brittle fracture modes. This mechanistic change represents a departure from grain-boundary embrittlement expectations seen in conventional alloys.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the role of deformation-induced local ordering in toughness loss, offering a decisive comparison between low- and room-temperature performance to confirm a novel embrittlement mechanism in HEAs.

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi HEA processed to ultra-fine grain sizes
proposals.intervention: High strain-rate deformation tests coupled with rapid microstructural quenching
proposals.conditions: Perform dynamic mechanical tests (e.g., split-Hopkinson pressure bar) at high strain rates followed by immediate cryo-fixation for TEM analysis
proposals.structural_mediator: Local, deformation-induced phase separation or transient nanophase formation
proposals.mechanism: At high strain rates, the high-entropy alloy may undergo localized phase separation driven by mechanical instabilities, resulting in transient nanophases or clusters that disrupt homogeneous plastic flow. These nanophases, though forming without full equilibrium precipitation, act as brittle zones that predispose the material to catastrophic failure, distinct from the slow grain-boundary coarsening seen in conventional alloys.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Specimens deformed at high strain rates will exhibit nanoscale structures (identified via TEM and diffraction) not present in quasi-static tests. These regions will correlate with embrittlement and reduced toughness under dynamic loading, effectively distinguishing this mechanism from conventional precipitate-driven embrittlement.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By comparing high strain-rate with quasi-static deformation, this test isolates a mechanically driven phase separation mechanism in HEAs, elucidating a unique pathway for toughness loss in these alloys.

proposals.material_system: Modified CoCrFeMnNi HEA with controlled trace impurity additions (e.g., small amounts of P or S)
proposals.intervention: Intentional doping with minute impurity levels followed by intermediate temperature aging
proposals.conditions: Introduce 0.1–0.5 wt% of impurity elements during alloy synthesis, then age at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., 400–600°C) under controlled atmospheres
proposals.structural_mediator: Nano-scale impurity segregation at defect sites and interfaces
proposals.mechanism: Even within a compositionally complex matrix, slight amounts of impurity can segregate to coherent interfaces or dislocation cores during aging. This segregation weakens local bonding, lowering ductility and toughness akin to classical impurity-induced grain-boundary embrittlement, but occurring in a single-phase HEA where other typical precipitates are absent.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples with controlled impurities will show enhanced impurity decoration at microstructural defects (confirmed via high-resolution TEM/EDS) and reduced toughness in fracture tests relative to a pure HEA baseline. Should the impurities not segregate or affect toughness, then the hypothesis would be falsified.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This study offers a controlled comparison by intentionally introducing potential embrittling agents, thereby testing if even minimal impurity segregation can trigger brittle behavior in HEAs—a mechanism that contrasts with common grain-boundary precipitation in conventional alloys.

decision.rationale: Direction A directly targets the question of how a single-phase HEA might develop brittle behavior by testing the role of trace impurity additions. By intentionally doping the alloy with minute amounts of elements like P or S and subsequently aging at service-relevant temperatures, this approach creates a controlled environment where impurity segregation at defect sites (e.g., dislocation cores or interfaces) can be directly correlated with reduced toughness. This mechanism contrasts with the conventional grain-boundary precipitation seen in traditional alloys, and the planned comparison with a pure HEA baseline provides a decisive test of whether even minimal impurity segregation can trigger embrittlement.
